amendments.why: PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 write nearly the same English clause — *But ... it is a N of N* — and take opposite treatments of the *it*. Rule 20 already rules that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added`, but rule 25's resumption paragraphs, widened to cover a referent denoted by a common noun rather than a pronoun, would let a later pass hand the expletive *it* of an extraposed clausal subject to the infinitive the ASV renders in full, since the verse does write that clause. The qualification belongs where the over-broad sentence stands rather than as a cross-reference from elsewhere. Inserted after the paragraph beginning *But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one*; the rest of rule 25 is returned unchanged.
amendments.rule: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁוַע` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **And where the Hebrew stands the pronoun is not part of the condition.** Hebrew postposes an explicit subject pronoun after its predicate and that predicate's adjuncts, often before a coordinated second subject, while English writes a subject before its verb; where the ASV writes the pronoun in both places it has realized one written morpheme twice, and both occurrences are that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first English occurrence: `וְהִנֵּה נִצָּב עַל־עֹלָתוֹ הוּא וְכָל־שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב` → *and lo* ***he*** *was standing by his burnt offering,* ***he*** *and all the princes of Moab* gives both *he*s to the one `הוּא`, while `נִצָּב` keeps the *was standing* rule 20 leaves it and the coordinated subject keeps its own English. So read whether one written pronoun is realized twice rather than which side of the resumption it stands on, and do not hand the first occurrence to the predicate to make the units contiguous: rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing a finite verb's own person and number, and a participle or other predicate morpheme in a verbless clause takes only the copula. **And the morpheme that denotes the resumed subject need not be a pronoun.** Where a common noun or a proper name written in the verse is the referent the ASV resumes, every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first English occurrence: `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ נוֹרָא הוֹד` → ***God*** *hath upon* ***him*** *terrible majesty* gives both *God* and *him* to the one `אֱלוֹהַּ`, and `שַׁדַּי לֹא־מְצָאנֻהוּ שַׂגִּיא־כֹּחַ` → *Touching* ***the Almighty****, we cannot find him out;* ***He*** *is excellent in power* gives the resuming *He* to `שַׁדַּי`, while `שַׂגִּיא` keeps the *is excellent* rule 20 leaves it. This is the preceding paragraphs' own reasoning read for the morpheme that is actually written — the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it — since what licenses the English word is that the verse writes the referent, and not the part of speech the ASV first realized it by. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהֶּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **But an expletive the ASV writes to fill a subject slot English cannot leave empty realizes no referent at all, whatever the verse writes.** Where the ASV extraposes a clausal subject the Hebrew writes — an infinitive phrase, or another clause the ASV renders in full further on — and puts an anticipatory *it* where that subject would stand, the pronoun denotes nothing the verse names and rule 20 governs it: it is its own `added` unit, while the predicate keeps the copula that rule gives it and the extraposed clause keeps its own English. `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → ***it*** *is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* leaves that *it* `added`, with *is an abomination* on the construct noun and *to depart* on the infinitive. What the sentences above place is a pronoun denoting a referent the verse names and the ASV has rendered by a word of its own, so read what the pronoun stands for before folding it into a written morpheme's unit: `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh,* ***it*** *is a tree of life* gives its *it* to `תַּאֲוָה`, which the ASV has already written as *the desire*, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 do. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once in the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.

conventions: An English *it* in a verbless clause is placed by what it stands for. The anaphoric *it* of `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life* (13.12) realizes `תַּאֲוָה`, which the verse writes and the ASV has already rendered *the desire*, and joins that noun's discontinuous unit under rule 25, the predicate keeping only *is a tree*. The anticipatory *it* of `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → *it is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* (13.19) fills a subject slot before an extraposed infinitival subject, denotes nothing the verse names, and is `added` under rule 20, the copula going to the nominal predicate. Read what the pronoun stands for, not the shape of the English clause; the two look alike.

A supplied possessive is `added` under rule 18's closing sentence even where its referent is written elsewhere in the verse: *his father's instruction* (13.1), *his folly* (13.16), *his children's children* (13.22) all leave the *his* `added`, because no possessive morpheme stands on the noun and rule 25's resumption reaches a pronoun realizing a referent's own syntactic slot, not a determiner supplied on some other noun. Contrast 13.2, where `אִישׁ` is itself the rectum of `פֶּה` and the ASV pronominalises it while promoting the same noun to subject: there *A man ... his* are both realizations of that one written morpheme.

A preposition the ASV supplies before a bare Hebrew nominal belongs to that nominal under rule 33 wherever the recasting leaves it an adjunct — *shall be to him that refuseth* (13.18), *recompensed with good* (13.21, where the passive makes the person the subject and `טוֹב` an adjunct of means), *is in the tillage* (13.23) — and to the verb under rule 44 only where the English verb reaches its own object through it, as *leaveth an inheritance to his children's children* (13.22). Ask what the nominal is in the English clause after the recasting, not what it was in the Hebrew.

The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amended.why: PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 write nearly the same English clause — *But ... it is a N of N* — and take opposite treatments of the *it*. Rule 20 already rules that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added`, but rule 25's resumption paragraphs, widened to cover a referent denoted by a common noun rather than a pronoun, would let a later pass hand the expletive *it* of an extraposed clausal subject to the infinitive the ASV renders in full, since the verse does write that clause. The qualification belongs where the over-broad sentence stands rather than as a cross-reference from elsewhere. Inserted after the paragraph beginning *But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one*; the rest of rule 25 is returned unchanged.

report: Checked all 31 candidate lemma groups. Every bucket with two treatments is the ASV rendering one word differently in a context the source licenses: waw (and / yet / But, read off the page under rule 14); huw' (possessive in 13.8, 13.24, 13.25 vs reflexive himself in 13.13); le (13.3 possessive le carrying *shall have* under rule 43 vs 13.13 a written *on*); nephesh (13.4's suffix unrendered because the appositional 'atsel holds the *of*-phrase); chakam (attributive in 13.1 vs substantival rectum in 13.14); ge'arah (*rebuke* / *threatening*); lo' (13.1 *not* vs 13.8 *no*, one construction and two ASV words, both placed on the negative); sur (13.14 has a purpose le to take the complementizer, 13.19 has no preposition and the infinitive holds its own *to* under rule 52); shama' and 'akal (mirrored gapping in 13.1 and 13.2, resolved identically under rule 34). No split among them.

Read the dump end to end for the splits the lemma table is blind to, which are the supplied-English ones. Supplied possessive *his*: added in 13.1, 13.16 and 13.22 under rule 18's closing sentence, and given to a written morpheme only in 13.2, where 'ish is itself the rectum of peh and the ASV pronominalises it - a licensed difference, not a split. Supplied *But*: added only in 13.3, the one colon with no waw in it. Supplied verbs: added only where no morpheme carries them (13.7's second *hath*, 13.11's *gotten*, 13.20's *for it*), never where one does (13.3 *shall have* on the possessive le, 13.4 and 13.7 *hath* on 'ayin under rule 50). English written twice for a gapped colon goes to the written morpheme every time, headed on the first English occurrence: 13.1 *heareth ... heareth*, 13.2 *shall eat ... shall eat*, 13.7 *There is ... There is*.

One real boundary, logged as a convention and carried into an amendment. PRO.13.12 *when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life* gives its *it* to ta'awah under rule 25's resumption sentences; PRO.13.19 *it is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* marks its *it* added under rule 20. The two English clauses look alike, the treatments are opposite, and both are right: the first *it* is anaphoric to a noun the verse writes and the ASV has already rendered, the second is an expletive filling a subject slot before an extraposed infinitival subject. Rule 25's recently widened resumption sentence is what would mislead a later pass into folding the second into the infinitive's unit, so the amendment goes there.

Second boundary, logged as a convention but not promoted: a supplied preposition before a bare Hebrew nominal. It is the nominal's under rule 33 wherever the ASV's recasting leaves that nominal an adjunct (13.18 *shall be to him that refuseth*, 13.21 *recompensed with good*, 13.23 *is in the tillage*), and the verb's under rule 44 only where the English verb reaches its own object through it (13.22 *leaveth an inheritance to his children's children*). 13.21 is the contestable one, since rule 44's *daubed with untempered mortar* is the same Hebrew shape read actively; the ASV's passive there makes tov an adjunct rather than the English verb's object, so the accepted edge stands. One instance is too thin to promote.

BSB: three disagreements, all convention differences, none an error. PRO.13.4 waw-suffix on naphsho - the ASV writes *The soul of the sluggard* with no possessive, and the written 'atsel holds the *of*-phrase, so the suffix is unrepresented under rule 22. PRO.13.13 le before davar - the ASV writes a bare English object, leaving the preposition nothing under rule 40. PRO.13.13 hu' - the resuming pronoun of a tripartite clause whose predicate is a written finite verb; the ASV realizes the subject once, in rule 46's supplied *he that* on the anarthrous yere', so the pronoun is unrepresented exactly as rule 20's tripartite sentence directs. Nothing here would be improved by moving an accepted edge.
No patches. 242 units, ledger clean, heads all members of their units; the chapter is internally consistent as it stands.
